edition.copy_text: Koetschau, GCS 2–3 (1899), via the Perseus TEI

source_text: Ἐπεὶ δὲ τοιαῦτα εἰπὼν ὁ Κέλσος περὶ τῶν διαφόρων νόμων ἐπιφέρει ὅτι ὀρθῶς μοι δοκεῖ Πίνδαρος ποιῆσαι, νόμον πάντων βασιλέα φήσας εἶναι, φέρε καὶ περὶ τούτου διαλεχθῶμεν. τίνα φῂς, ὦ οὗτος, νόμον πάντων εἶναι βασιλέα; εἰ μὲν τοὺς κατὰ πόλιν, ψεῦδος τὸ τοιοῦτον· οὐ γὰρ ὑπὸ τοῦ αὐτοῦ νόμου πάντες βασιλεύονται· καὶ χρῆν, εἰ ἄρα, λελέχθαι· νόμοι πάντων βασιλεῖς, ἑκάστου γὰρ ἔθνους τῶν πάντων νόμος τις βασιλεύς. εἰ δὲ κυρίως ἀκούεις τοῦ νόμου, ὁ φύσει βασιλεὺς τῶν πάντων οὗτός ἐστιν· εἰ καί τινες δίκην λῃστῶν, ἀποστάντων τοῦ νόμου. τοῦτον μὲν ἀρνοῦνται λῃστρικῶς δὲ καὶ ἀδικητικῶς διαζῶσιν. ἡμεῖς οὖν οἱ Χριστιανοὶ τὸν τῇ φύσει πάντων βασιλέα ἐπιγνόντες νόμον, τὸν αὐτὸν ὄντα τῷ νόμῳ τοῦ θεοῦ, κατ᾿ αὐτὸν βιοῦν πειρώμεθα, μακρὰν χαίρειν φράσαντες τοῖς οὐ νόμοις νόμοις.
thought_title: Which law is king of all
pass_a_gloss: Since Celsus, having said such things about the different laws, adds that 'Pindar seems to me to have composed rightly, having said law is king of all,' come, let us converse/discuss about this too. What law do you say, you there, is king of all? If those according to city, such a thing is a falsehood; for not by the same law are all ruled as by a king; and it ought, if at all, to have been said: 'laws are kings of all', for of each nation of all some law is king. But if you hear/understand 'law' properly, this is by nature king of all; even if some, in the manner of robbers who have stood off/revolted from the law, deny this and live through robber-like and unjustly. We then the Christians, having recognised the law king of all by nature, being the same as the law of God, try to live according to it, having bidden far farewell to the not-laws laws.

pass_b_english: After saying such things about the different laws, Celsus adds: “Pindar seems to me to have been right when he wrote that law is king of all” (Pindar, fragment 169). Come, then, let us discuss this too. What law, my friend, do you say is king of all? If you mean the laws of the several cities, the statement is false, for not all people are ruled by the same law. In that case it ought to have been said, if at all, “Laws are kings of all,” since over each nation of them all some law is king.

But if you take law in its proper sense, this law is by nature king of all, even if some, like robbers who have revolted from the law, deny it and live like robbers and wrongdoers. We Christians, then, having come to know the law that is by nature king of all, which is the same as the law of God, try to live according to it, and have bidden a long farewell to the laws that are not laws.
notes: Pindar's line νόμος ὁ πάντων βασιλεύς is fragment 169 (Snell-Maehler 169a); it is also quoted by Herodotus 3.38 and Plato, Gorgias 484b. Celsus's sentence is given as a direct quotation (the ὅτι is recitative and μοι is first person). ὦ οὗτος is a brusque address ('you there'), softened to 'my friend' (reviewer: 'my good man' dropped as dated). οἱ κατὰ πόλιν νόμοι = the laws of the individual cities/states. The punctuation of the Perseus text (period after νόμου, then τοῦτον μὲν ἀρνοῦνται) breaks one sentence; it is read as one concessive clause. οὐ νόμοι νόμοι ('laws that are not laws') is an idiom of the type 'a gift that is no gift'. The thought of a law 'by nature' recalls Romans 2:14-15, but there is no verbal echo, so no inline citation is given.
